cells.tense: You are standing where something has finished, and you can let it be finished.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you gave up for this, plainly, then put your hands on the next task. That's the whole act.
cells.core:
You know what this ending costs and you're not dressing it up. The people around you can see the effort underneath it, which is why their thanks land instead of sliding off. You don't need the room to declare it was worth it before you'll close the door. You pick up what comes next without dragging the old thing behind you.

The care hasn't hardened into grip. You keep what's left without clutching it, and that doesn't wear you out. What keeps this steady is that you let the ending be an ending — a task finished, a goodbye said properly, then your attention on something new. The praise stays real because you take it in rather than carrying it around as proof.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a goodbye that hasn't arrived yet and doesn't need you to arrive with it.
cells.ask: Pick one loose end and close it this week — one call, one box — before it costs you another night of planning.
cells.core:
You're living ahead of the ending, rehearsing it, planning how people will take it and how you'll come off when it's done. The work itself gets skipped, because you're busy managing a farewell that hasn't happened. People can feel you halfway out of the room, and you're not even sure you're leaving.

It shows up small first: the message you draft and don't send, the account you mean to settle, the thank-you rehearsed into a speech. When release is working, it's just the next honest step — finishing that feels like finishing, not a defeat you survive. The arranging is doing the opposite. Try closing one thing before you're sure it's time.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, waiting for someone to come and open it.
cells.ask: Finish one thing you stopped halfway through. Tell no one. Leave it where it lands.
cells.core:
Something ended and part of you hasn't moved past it. You're polite, functional, but you talk about the old thing in the present tense, and the new thing hasn't started. Nothing is wrong with the ground you're on. You just haven't stepped off it.

It isn't unwillingness. Saying the goodbye plainly, without softening it, feels like work you don't have in you right now, so you stay near the old thing and being near it passes for handling it. Finishing something hard is a strength you build, and building it back doesn't mean pushing into the emptiness. One small completion, no commentary attached, is enough to stand on.

cells.tense: You are already clearing things away and closing old business, and you describe it as simply getting on with it.
cells.ask: Name one cleanup you'd call regular housekeeping as an ending, and tell someone it closed a chapter.
cells.core:
You're the one ending things, and the endings are good ones — the file deleted, the habit quietly dropped, the old commitment wound down. You file it under being practical. But you're the one who decided, and that decision is doing real work. A door has closed somewhere and you're treating it like nothing happened.

People around you see the shift, even if they don't name it. What the clearing wants is to be owned rather than filed under chores. Tending what comes next works when it grows without being forced — care that doesn't exhaust. Turning one of those practical moves into a stated ending isn't ceremony. It's the difference between tidying and knowing what you've put down.

attempts.check: The one claim the record does not support: that the person is ending something specifically — the seat is Transformation, but the plain life may have no ending in view, so every cell must describe the capacity bending (grip on the goodbye, still standing at one, steering the clearing) without asserting what is ending. The reader could reasonably object 'no one is asking me to let go of anything' — so the asks are acts anyone can do today with no audience and no props, and they stay useful if the read is wrong by handing a real interaction or a real hour back. The sentence that serves the writer is the Too Much core's 'the looking isn't landing': it flatters the diagnosis; keep it but let the failure live in the moment, not in the person's motives, and never quote it on a sheet line.

A reader could reasonably say 'nothing is ending, I'm just tired of a project' — so the asks are plain acts anyone can do today with no audience, props, money or free time, and they stay useful even if the read is wrong because each one produces information about what the person is actually still holding. The sentence that serves the writer is Too Much's 'you're managing a farewell that hasn't happened' — it diagnoses and flatters; hold the failure in the rehearsing and the drafting, never in the person's character, and keep it out of the sheet lines.
